_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- New York rule seed, 2026-08-24. Loaded through add_rule.
Every provision below was read VERBATIM before being encoded: the CPLR and the
General Construction Law from Justia's published New York Consolidated Laws (2025
edition) and, for CPLR 320 and CPLR 3120, from the New York State Senate's own
legislation site. CPLR 2103(b) was read in full, all seven paragraphs.
THE COMPUTATION RULE IS NOT IN THE CPLR. This is the structural thing about New
York and it has no parallel anywhere else in this engine. Every other jurisdiction
computes time under the same body of rules that sets its deadlines -- FRCP 6(a) for
the FRCP, Tex. R. Civ. P. 4 for the TRCP, and so on. The CPLR has no such provision
at all. The arithmetic comes from a different statute entirely:
N.Y. Gen. Constr. Law 20    counting
N.Y. Gen. Constr. Law 25-a  what happens when the last day is bad
N.Y. Gen. Constr. Law 24    what counts as a public holiday
And the link is express, unlike the Texas one. Gen. Constr. Law 110: 'This chapter
is applicable to every statute unless its general object, or the context of the
language construed, or other provisions of law indicate that a different meaning or
application was intended from that required to be given by this chapter.' The CPLR
is a statute and indicates no different application. Recorded because the Texas seed
had to disclose the OPPOSITE -- Tex. R. Civ. P. 4 says 'legal holiday' and never
cites a definition -- and the two should not be assumed to stand on the same footing.
GEN. CONSTR. LAW 20'S TWO-DAY LIMB IS DELIBERATELY NOT DECLARED, and this is a
judgment call rather than an omission. The sentence -- 'If such period is a period of
two days, Saturday, Sunday or a public holiday must be excluded from the reckoning if
it is an intervening day' -- looks like the short-period exclusion Ohio, Indiana,
Florida and Texas all have, and the reflex is to set short_period_exclusion_days.
That would misstate it twice over: the engine's property means 'every period shorter
than N' where section 20 means EXACTLY two, and the other four states exclude such
days from the count where section 20 excludes only an INTERVENING day on a two-day
span. No New York rule seeded here has a two-day period (the shortest is 20), so the
limb is unreachable either way. Contrast Texas, whose equally unreachable threshold IS
declared, because there the rule's mechanism and the engine's property genuinely match.
THE SERVICE EXTENSION IS PER-METHOD, AND ONE AMOUNT IS IN BUSINESS DAYS.
CPLR 2103(b)(2) adds FIVE days for mail within the state and SIX for mail from
outside the state but within the United States. CPLR 2103(b)(6) adds ONE BUSINESS DAY
for overnight delivery -- the first business-day extension in this engine. One
business day is not one calendar day: overnight service on a Friday lands on Monday,
and more across a holiday weekend. Counting it as a calendar day would produce a date
EARLIER than the true deadline.
A bare 'mail' is REJECTED, as in California, because the amount depends on where the
mailing was made. And a mailing from OUTSIDE the United States gets no entry at all:
2103(b)(2) provides five in-state and six from elsewhere in the US and then stops. It
states no amount for a foreign mailing. California's CCP 1013(a) does address that and
gives 20 days; borrowing that number here would be inventing New York law, so such a
method draws a visible refusal instead.
NO ADDED DAYS FOR FAX OR ELECTRONIC SERVICE. CPLR 2103(b)(5) and (b)(7) each define
when that service is complete and neither adds time -- only (b)(2) and (b)(6) carry an
added-days clause. This is the available mistake in New York practice, because
e-filing feels like it ought to behave like mail. Any contrary provision in the rules
of the chief administrator that (b)(7) refers to was NOT read for this seed, so
nothing is assumed in either direction.
CPLR 5513(d) IS THE MIRROR IMAGE OF CALIFORNIA, AND IS WORTH SEEING SIDE BY SIDE.
California's CCP 1013 and 1010.6(a)(3)(B) both say in terms that the extension 'shall
not apply to extend the time for filing ... a notice of appeal', so all three of the
California appellate rows carry no extension. New York says the opposite, expressly:
5513(d) provides that where the judgment and notice of entry are served by mail under
2103(b)(2) or by overnight delivery under 2103(b)(6), 'the additional days provided by
such paragraphs shall apply to this action, regardless of which party serves the
judgment or order with notice of entry.' So the New York appeal rows DO carry the
extension. Carrying the California instinct across a state line loses five days of an
appeal period; carrying the New York instinct the other way invents five.
THE APPEAL TRIGGER IS SERVICE OF NOTICE OF ENTRY, NOT ENTRY, NOT SIGNING, NOT
RENDITION. Four jurisdictions in this engine now start an appeal clock four different
ways -- Texas from the SIGNING of the judgment, Florida from RENDITION, California
from service of a notice of entry (or 180 days from entry), New York from service of
a copy of the judgment WITH written notice of its entry. A user who supplies an entry
date to a New York row gets a wrong answer, and the engine cannot tell.
5513(a) HAS TWO LIMBS AND THEY ARE SEPARATE ROWS. The ordinary limb runs from service
BY ANOTHER PARTY upon the appellant. The 'except that' limb runs from the appellant's
OWN service of the judgment with notice of entry. Both are thirty days, both run from
a service event, and which applies depends on who served -- a case fact the engine has
no field for. Two triggers, so the caller must say.
CPLR 3120(2) SETS NO DEADLINE, IT SETS A FLOOR, and is encoded as a designated-period
rule rather than as a twenty-day deadline. The notice or subpoena duces tecum 'shall
specify the time, which shall be not less than twenty days after service'. The
operative date is whatever the requesting party actually specified; twenty is only the
minimum a valid notice may demand. Same shape as Ohio's and Indiana's discovery rules,
and the same reason: stating the floor as though it were the deadline answers a
question nobody asked and is wrong whenever the notice allowed longer, which is most
of the time. Note this is NOT the same as CPLR 3122(a)(1), which is a real twenty-day
deadline for OBJECTING and is its own row -- New York splits the objection deadline
from the production date, and conflating them would be wrong in both directions.
NOT ENCODED, deliberately, and flagged rather than dropped:
1. CPLR 5513(c), the cross-appeal limb: a party served with a notice of appeal may
appeal 'within ten days after such service or within the time limited by
subdivision (a) or (b) of this section, whichever is longer.' One limb is a period
this engine itself computed rather than an event date, so the multi-trigger shape,
which resolves between supplied DATES, cannot express it. Exactly the same class as
Tex. R. App. P. 26.1(d), Ohio App.R. 4(B)(1) and FRCP 15(a)(3). Named, not
improvised.
2. CPLR 5513(b), permission to appeal. Thirty days computed the same way, but it is a
motion rather than an appeal as of right and its trigger vocabulary differs by
posture (including a prior denial); left for a later phase rather than approximated.
3. The CPLR 320(a) and 3012(c) thirty-day clocks run from when 'service is complete',
which for CPLR 308(2) and 308(4) is a computed date -- service is complete a fixed
number of days after proof of service is filed. THE ENGINE TAKES THE COMPLETION DATE
AS GIVEN AND DOES NOT COMPUTE IT. CPLR 308 was not read verbatim for this seed, so
no completion arithmetic is encoded and none is guessed. A user who supplies the
delivery date instead of the completion date will get a date that is too early. This
is the single most dangerous input error available in the New York set and it is
flagged on both rows.
4. Days appointed by the PRESIDENT or the GOVERNOR as days of general thanksgiving,
fasting and prayer or other general religious observances -- public holidays under
Gen. Constr. Law 24 and unknowable in advance. Same class as Illinois's
Governor-proclamation limb, Indiana's office-closed limb, Florida's chief-justice
hurricane limb, California's CCP 12b and Texas's Tex. R. App. P. 4.1(b).
5. Gen. Constr. Law 24's half-holiday (noon to midnight of each Saturday that is not a
public holiday). A partial day; this engine counts whole days, and Saturdays are
excluded by 25-a regardless.
6. Gen. Constr. Law 25-a's application to BACKWARD-counted periods. Its opening reaches
a period 'before which' an act is required, but its only remedy is 'the next
succeeding business day', which for a backward period would push the deadline past
the event it is measured against. Unresolved by the text; no backward New York rule
is seeded and the standard's backward suffix is left blank rather than citing 25-a
for behaviour it does not describe.
7. CPLR 3012(b)'s demand-for-complaint chain, and 3012(d)'s discretionary extension.
The first is a multi-step interaction between two parties' elections rather than a
single period; the second is a court order the engine cannot see.
8. CPLR 3122(a)(2)'s medical-provider subpoena carve-out -- a condition on whether a
response is owed at all, not a different period.
EFFECTIVE DATES. Every row carries the effective date of the amendment that set the
period where the source prints one, and otherwise the date of the published edition
read (2025), following the Florida convention. A New York matter whose period runs
from before a row's effective_from is REFUSED rather than computed against text that
was never read -- the same call already made for Pennsylvania, Florida and Texas.

rules.label: Appearance after personal delivery of the summons within the state (New York)

authority.quote: The defendant appears by serving an answer or a notice of appearance, or by making a motion which has the effect of extending the time to answer. An appearance shall be made within twenty days after service of the summons, except that if the summons was served on the defendant by delivering it to an official of the state authorized to receive service in his behalf or if it was served pursuant to section 303, subdivision two, three, four or five of section 308, or sections 313, 314 or 315, the appearance shall be made within thirty days after service is complete.
authority.note: THE TWENTY-DAY PERIOD IS THE EXCEPTION IN PRACTICE, NOT THE RULE. It applies only where the summons was personally delivered to the defendant within the state under CPLR 308(1); every alternative method named in the quoted text carries thirty days instead, and is a separate row. Which one applies is a case fact the engine has no field for. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: CPLR 2103(b) governs service of papers 'upon an attorney' in a pending action, and this clock runs from service of process, so the 2103(b)(2) five days do not reach it. NOT encoded: CPLR 3012(b)'s demand-for-complaint chain, which can extend the time to appear, and 3012(d)'s discretionary extension. Note also that this is the APPEARANCE deadline; the deadline to serve an ANSWER is CPLR 3012 and is its own row.

rules.label: Appearance where the summons was not personally delivered in state, measured from completion of service (New York)

authority.quote: if the summons was served on the defendant by delivering it to an official of the state authorized to receive service in his behalf or if it was served pursuant to section 303, subdivision two, three, four or five of section 308, or sections 313, 314 or 315, the appearance shall be made within thirty days after service is complete.
authority.note: THE TRIGGER IS THE DATE SERVICE IS COMPLETE, NOT THE DATE OF DELIVERY, AND THE ENGINE DOES NOT COMPUTE IT. For CPLR 308(2) leave-and-mail and 308(4) affix-and-mail, service is complete a fixed number of days after proof of service is filed, so the completion date is later than the delivery date and often by more than a week. CPLR 308 was NOT read verbatim for this seed and no completion arithmetic is encoded here; the date supplied is used as given. A user who supplies the delivery date will get a deadline that is TOO EARLY, which is the safe direction to be wrong but is still wrong -- and if they supply the filing date instead they will be too early by a different amount. This is the most dangerous input error in the New York set. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: this clock runs from service of process, not from service of a paper on an attorney under CPLR 2103(b).

rules.label: Answer or reply to a pleading served in a pending action (New York)

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CPLR 2103(b)(2) adds 5 CALENDAR days for mail within the state and 6 for mail from outside the state but within the United States, and CPLR 2103(b)(6) adds 1 BUSINESS day for overnight delivery. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted.

authority.quote: Service of an answer or reply shall be made within twenty days after service of the pleading to which it responds.
authority.note: THIS IS THE PLEADING-RESPONSE CLOCK AND IT IS NOT THE APPEARANCE CLOCK. CPLR 320(a) governs when the defendant must APPEAR; this governs when an answer or reply must be SERVED. Both can be live in the same matter on different dates. It covers a reply to a counterclaim as well as an answer to a complaint, which is why the trigger names the pleading responded to rather than the complaint. SERVICE EXTENSION DOES APPLY here, unlike the two CPLR 320 rows: the pleading is a paper served in a pending action under CPLR 2103, which is exactly what 2103(b)(2) and (b)(6) reach. Where the summons and complaint were NOT personally delivered in state, CPLR 3012(c) gives thirty days from completion of service instead and is a separate row.

rules.label: Answer where the summons and complaint were not personally delivered in state, measured from completion of service (New York)

authority.quote: If the complaint is served with the summons and the service is made on the defendant by delivering the summons and complaint to an official of the state authorized to receive service in his behalf or if service of the summons and complaint is made pursuant to section 303, paragraphs two, three, four or five of section 308, or sections 313, 314 or 315, service of an answer shall be made within thirty days after service is complete.
authority.note: Parallel to the CPLR 320(a) thirty-day row and subject to the SAME trigger hazard: the clock runs from when service is COMPLETE, which for CPLR 308(2) and 308(4) is a computed date later than delivery. The engine takes that date as given and does not compute it -- CPLR 308 was not read verbatim for this seed. Note the condition here is narrower than 320(a)'s in one respect the quoted text makes explicit: it applies only where the complaint was served WITH the summons. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: the clock runs from service of process, not from service of a paper on an attorney.

rules.label: Answers or objections to interrogatories (New York)

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CPLR 2103(b)(2) adds 5 CALENDAR days for mail within the state and 6 for mail from outside the state but within the United States, and CPLR 2103(b)(6) adds 1 BUSINESS day for overnight delivery. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted.

authority.quote: Within twenty days after service of interrogatories, the party upon whom they are served shall serve upon each of the parties a copy of the answer to each interrogatory, except one to which the party objects, in which event the reasons for the objection shall be stated with reasonable particularity.
authority.note: TWENTY DAYS, NOT THIRTY. Every other jurisdiction in this engine that sets a real interrogatory-response deadline sets thirty -- federal, Florida, California, Texas and Michigan among them -- and Ohio and Indiana set no deadline at all. New York is the outlier at twenty, and a practitioner carrying a thirty-day habit across the state line is ten days late. A REAL DEADLINE, unlike Ohio's and Indiana's designated-period floors: the date this produces is a genuine due date. Note the answer and any objection share one deadline here; New York does not split them the way it splits the CPLR 3120 production date from the CPLR 3122 objection date.

rules.label: Objection to a notice to produce or subpoena duces tecum (New York)

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CPLR 2103(b)(2) adds 5 CALENDAR days for mail within the state and 6 for mail from outside the state but within the United States, and CPLR 2103(b)(6) adds 1 BUSINESS day for overnight delivery. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted.

authority.quote: Within twenty days of service of a notice or subpoena duces tecum under rule 3120 or section 3121, the party or person to whom the notice or subpoena duces tecum is directed, if that party or person objects to the disclosure, inspection or examination, shall serve a response which shall state with reasonable particularity the reasons for each objection.
authority.note: THIS IS THE OBJECTION DEADLINE, NOT THE PRODUCTION DATE, AND NEW YORK GENUINELY SPLITS THEM. The date documents must actually be produced is whatever the notice specified under CPLR 3120(2), which may be far later than twenty days and is a separate designated-period row. Treating this twenty days as the production deadline would be wrong early; treating the production date as the objection deadline would forfeit objections. No other jurisdiction in this engine splits the two this way. Note it binds a non-party served with a subpoena duces tecum as well as a party. NOT encoded: 3122(a)(2)'s medical-provider carve-out, which conditions whether a response is owed at all rather than changing the period.

rules.label: Production under a notice to produce, on the date the notice designated (New York)

designated_period.designated_by: the party serving the notice or subpoena duces tecum

authority.quote: the time, which shall be not less than twenty days after service
authority.note: SETS NO DEADLINE, SETS A FLOOR. The notice or subpoena duces tecum specifies the time for production, and twenty days is only the minimum a valid notice may demand. The operative date is whatever the requesting party actually specified, so the engine asks for it and refuses a designation below the floor rather than quietly computing twenty. Same shape and same reasoning as Ohio's Civ.R. 33(A)/36(A)(1) and Indiana's T.R. 33(C)/36(A). Any tool returning a flat twenty days for a New York notice to produce is answering a question the rule does not ask. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, and that is enforced by the engine rather than chosen here: a designated-period rule cannot carry one, because the designated figure already is the period and adding days to a party-chosen period would extend a deadline the rule never set.

rules.label: Sworn denial before a requested admission is deemed admitted (New York)

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CPLR 2103(b)(2) adds 5 CALENDAR days for mail within the state and 6 for mail from outside the state but within the United States, and CPLR 2103(b)(6) adds 1 BUSINESS day for overnight delivery. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted.

authority.quote: Each of the matters of which an admission is requested shall be deemed admitted unless within twenty days after service thereof or within such further time as the court may allow, the party to whom the request is directed serves upon the party requesting the admission a sworn statement either denying specifically the matters of which an admission is requested or setting forth in detail the reasons why he cannot truthfully either admit or deny those matters.
authority.note: SELF-EXECUTING AND ONLY TWENTY DAYS -- the shortest deemed-admission window in this engine, against thirty in Illinois, Florida and Texas. Missing it admits the matter by operation of the rule with no motion and no order, the same shape as Ill. S. Ct. R. 216(c), Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.370(a)(6) and Tex. R. Civ. P. 198.2(c), and expressly NOT the California shape, where the deemed-admitted consequence runs through a separate motion under CCP 2033.280. The combination of the shortest period and the harshest automatic consequence makes this the most consequential deadline in the New York civil set. NOTE THE RESPONSE MUST BE A SWORN STATEMENT: an unsworn denial served on time does not satisfy the rule on its face, and the engine computes only the date. The 'or within such further time as the court may allow' clause is a court-order escape the engine cannot see. CPLR 3123(b) separately lets the court allow amendment or withdrawal of an admission.

rules.label: Appeal as of right, measured from another party's service of the judgment with notice of entry (New York)

service_extension.note: Attached on the express authority of CPLR 5513(d), which provides that where the judgment and notice of entry are served by mail under 2103(b)(2) or by overnight delivery under 2103(b)(6), the additional days provided by those paragraphs apply, regardless of which party served. Amount and unit come from the standard: 5 CALENDAR days for mail within the state, 6 for mail from outside the state but within the United States, 1 BUSINESS day for overnight delivery.

authority.quote: An appeal as of right must be taken within thirty days after service by a party upon the appellant of a copy of the judgment or order appealed from and written notice of its entry ... Where service of the judgment or order to be appealed from and written notice of its entry is made by mail pursuant to paragraph two of subdivision (b) of rule twenty-one hundred three or by overnight delivery service pursuant to paragraph six of subdivision (b) of rule twenty-one hundred three of this chapter, the additional days provided by such paragraphs shall apply to this action, regardless of which party serves the judgment or order with notice of entry.
authority.note: THE TRIGGER IS SERVICE OF THE JUDGMENT TOGETHER WITH WRITTEN NOTICE OF ITS ENTRY -- not entry, not signing, not rendition. Four jurisdictions here now start an appeal clock four different ways: Texas from the SIGNING of the judgment, Florida from RENDITION, California from service of a notice of entry or 180 days from entry, New York from this. Supplying an entry date to this row produces a wrong answer the engine cannot detect. THE SERVICE EXTENSION APPLIES, AND THAT IS THE EXPRESS OPPOSITE OF CALIFORNIA, where CCP 1013 and 1010.6(a)(3)(B) both exclude a notice of appeal from the extension in terms. 5513(d) is quoted above precisely so the contrast is on the record. Where the APPELLANT was the one who served, the 'except that' limb of 5513(a) governs instead and is a separate row.

rules.label: Appeal as of right where the appellant served the judgment with notice of entry (New York)

service_extension.note: Attached on the express authority of CPLR 5513(d), whose closing words -- 'regardless of which party serves the judgment or order with notice of entry' -- reach this limb specifically. Amount and unit come from the standard: 5 CALENDAR days for mail within the state, 6 for mail from outside the state but within the United States, 1 BUSINESS day for overnight delivery.

authority.quote: except that when the appellant has served a copy of the judgment or order and written notice of its entry, the appeal must be taken within thirty days thereof.
authority.note: A DIFFERENT CLOCK FROM A DIFFERENT EVENT, which is why it is its own row: the ordinary limb runs from service BY ANOTHER PARTY upon the appellant, this one from the appellant's OWN service. Both are thirty days, so the difference is invisible in the number and lives entirely in which date starts it -- a party who serves notice of entry to start the other side's clock starts their own at the same moment, and it is easy to assume only the recipient's clock runs. Which limb applies is a case fact the engine has no field for and never infers. 5513(d)'s 'regardless of which party serves' clause is what makes the service extension apply on this limb too.

rules.label: Appeal or motion for permission by a party served with a notice of appeal, the later of ten days and the subdivision (a) period (New York)

limbs.label: 10 days after service of the adverse party's notice of appeal or motion papers
30 days after service of the judgment with written notice of entry, the subdivision (a) period

authority.quote: A party upon whom the adverse party has served a notice of appeal or motion papers on a motion for permission to appeal may take an appeal or make a motion for permission to appeal within ten days after such service or within the time limited by subdivision (a) or (b) of this section, whichever is longer, if such appeal or motion is otherwise available to such party.
authority.note: NOW COMPUTABLE. Refused by this engine until 2026-08-24: the limbs carry different counts (10 and 30) from different events, which the older date-resolving multi-trigger shape could not express. "Whichever is longer" is the rule's own language here, unlike Ohio's App.R. 4(B)(1), which says only "or". LIMB TWO IS THE SUBDIVISION (a) PERIOD IN ITS ORDINARY FORM -- 30 days after another party served the judgment with written notice of entry. The quoted text says "subdivision (a) OR (b)", and (b) is the permission-to-appeal period, which is also thirty days but runs from a different event and has its own posture including a prior denial. No (b) variant is seeded; which subdivision governs is a case fact. Nor is a variant seeded for 5513(a)'s own "except that" limb, where the appellant served the notice of entry themselves. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, and that is a deliberate departure from the two 5513(a) rows either side of it. CPLR 5513(d) attaches the 2103(b)(2) and (b)(6) added days by name to service of "the judgment or order to be appealed from and written notice of its entry" -- it does not mention service of a NOTICE OF APPEAL, which is what starts limb one. Extending one limb and not the other on a comparison of two periods is not something 5513(d) authorises on its face, so none is attached and the row produces the earlier, safer date. Flagged rather than silently resolved.
